title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200); every initial candidate passed the validator, so no repair calls were issued. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank under the frozen shared‑initial policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the sealed preregistered design, reconciled determinism/accounting evidence from the archived execution bundle, holdout emulator corroboration for a 10% sample that found no validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Generative language models can translate high‑level operator intent into network configuration actions, promising productivity gains but also posing risks of incorrect or unsafe changes. Prior work proposes grounding and verifier‑assisted repair loops (generate–validate–repair, or GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the practical benefit of automated repair depends on baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures, validator coverage and fidelity, and the repair budget and prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question to isolate one operational contrast: when the generator output is fixed per task, does invoking a deterministic validator—and at most one automated repair prompt if the validator reports violations—reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect changes relative to applying the generator output unchecked? The paired, shared‑initial design fixes the generator output for both conditions and therefore isolates the marginal effect of validation+repair on that identical candidate.
sections.related_work: LLMs for NetOps have been explored in prototypes that perform intent→configuration translation and in surveys that document hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism. Mitigations proposed in the literature include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained agent architectures, and guarded tool registries. Work on verifier‑assisted pipelines and Batfish‑style checkers motivates our focus; complementary red‑team studies document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that increase attack surface. Our study contributes an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validation+repair for a fixed generation policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistration (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were bootstrap percentile intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. The confirmatory sample comprised a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final state plus workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal validator blind spots.

Determinism and adapter enforcement (review reconciliation). The model configuration artifact records the declared model and requested settings (declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" and a model_configuration entry with a null temperature field). Determinism in this run was not achieved by setting an explicit temperature parameter in the model configuration; instead, the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics so that, for each task, a single generator invocation was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. Evidence for this enforcement is present in the archived adapter/provider accounting artifacts: deterministic_reconciliation.json (provider_call_audit.hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 200}) and the execution audit fields that report completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200. These artifacts show single shared invocations per task and therefore a removal of sampling variance across conditions; the adapter‑level semantics—not an in‑model temperature override recorded in model_configuration—deliver the controlled paired contrast. The bootstrap parameters and seed for the CI procedure are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Execution contract and repair policy. The execution contract limited model calls to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); the adapter enforced this cap. If the primary validator reported violations, the preregistered policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; repaired candidates would be re‑validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and recorded. Missingness/exclusion rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure execution failures; tasks flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would have been excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan.

Reproducibility pointers. The archived execution bundle contains canonical artifacts for auditing the run (examples: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, deterministic_reconciliation.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Detailed provenance and the artifact manifest are archived with the preregistration. We intentionally avoid low‑level file dumps in this prose and provide the concise canonical artifact list above for inspection.
sections.results:
Accounting and adapter audit. Execution completed all planned episodes and pairs: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter/provider auditing fields in deterministic_reconciliation.json report hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task and that no repair calls were consumed.

Validator outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200 and guarded_success_count = 200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). With no discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable because baseline validator failures are absent on this sample.

Repair and contamination. No validator failures were observed, so the repair branch was never invoked and secondary estimands (repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per repair) are empty in the archived analysis artifacts. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% randomized sample) produced no validator–emulator disagreements per analysis/contamination_summary.csv.

Representative diagnostics. Representative per‑task validator traces (archived scoring artifacts for sample pairs) show validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 while exercising nontrivial required_sequence and dependency constraints (difficulty labels include "medium", "hard", "very_hard" and patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). These artifacts demonstrate that the task bank included complex workflow constraints even though the generator produced validator‑satisfying sequences under the frozen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate paired outcome (no discordant pairs) is an artifact‑grounded empirical result: under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy and with the chosen model and prompt policy, validator‑detectable failures were absent on our curated task bank. This does not prove that GVR is never useful; it precisely states that, on this workload and under this strict pairing design, there were no validator‑detectable failures for the GVR pipeline to reduce.

Why the null occurred. Adapter accounting and per‑task validator traces explain the null: (i) the shared_initial design fixed generator outputs per task and removed sampling variance; (ii) the generator+prompt policy produced outputs that satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints encoded by the validator (parsed_command_count matched required_command_count across representative traces); and (iii) the Mininet holdout found no validator–emulator disagreements in the sampled 20 tasks. The archived artifacts referenced above document each of these points.

Methodological tradeoffs and recommendations. The shared_initial paired design provides a controlled causal contrast at the cost of excluding gains obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM (e.g., drawing alternative candidates that a repair routine could operate on). For settings where unconditional failure prevalence matters, we recommend mixed designs that include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws, larger repair budgets (multi‑step repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation), stronger secondary emulation coverage, and multi‑model comparisons. These directions are compatible with the preregistered execution template captured in the archived bundle.

Validator coverage and operational implications. Deterministic validators codify a testable subset of safety constraints; they are necessary but not sufficient oracles for full operational safety. The Mininet holdout is a pragmatic secondary check but its scale and the absence of a labeled holdout selection seed in the archive limit the strength of generalization; the contamination summary nevertheless reports zero disagreements for the sampled tasks. Practitioners should therefore prioritize (1) measuring baseline validator failure prevalence on representative, production‑like workloads, and (2) expanding validator fidelity (vendor semantics, device models) and emulation/testbed sampling to probe blind spots before relying solely on a single repair pass.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), resulting in an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. This artifact‑grounded outcome shows that GVR’s marginal value depends on workload and baseline failure prevalence: where validator‑detectable failures are rare under the intended generation policy, a single automated repair pass yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should sample workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator and emulator coverage, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore larger or human‑assisted repair budgets to quantify practical operational gains. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived under the preregistration id cited above for independent inspection.

A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the archived contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
